prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it

statement.case_for: I keep B025 as my single final position and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. The chair's summary sharpens what is being credited: the existence of correlated insulating and gate-tunable superconducting phases at the magic angle, predicted by the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model and found by Jarillo-Herrero's group in 2018. As an experimentalist I find this the most secure feature of the case. It does not rest on an interpretation. The phases appear in transport in many independent laboratories and in several moire platforms, and no one has reported conflicting results on their existence. That is a different situation from a contested measurement. The pairing mechanism is a separate and open theoretical question, and a citation that stays on the flat-band prediction and the first correlated and superconducting states neither claims nor depends on it. Of the three leading candidates this is the one that opened a regime of electronic matter that was previously unknown and is controlled by a single geometric parameter, and eight years of replication across groups is, in my judgement, enough to separate the established core from the fast-moving surrounding literature.
statement.case_against: Timing and attribution remain the real weaknesses, and I do not want to discount them because four of us agree. B025 is the youngest of the three leading cases. Twist-angle disorder still makes sample-to-sample behaviour uneven, and a committee that put weight on settled interpretation would reasonably prefer B013, which has nearly two decades of confirmation behind it. Attribution is also not clean in either direction: Eva Andrei's early scanning-probe evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities at small twist angles is a credible experimental claim, and the three-name cap forces one of four people with documented contributions out. The topological-insulator case (B013) has its own compound-credit problem with Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, and the lattice-clock case (B006) is the cleanest on names but is the one where the novelty question against the 2005 and 2012 prizes is most open. Whichever way the committee goes, it will be leaving out a serious claimant or a serious objection.

responses.point: Lindroth accepts that B025 has the broadest support but does not equate wide replication of the phenomenology with maturity, citing the unresolved pairing mechanism, strain and twist-angle disorder, and the Andrei priority question as a serious experimental claim, not a footnote.
responses.response: I accept that Andrei's claim is a priority question and not a footnote, and I accept that the choice between her and Bistritzer is the most contestable seat. Where I differ is in what maturity should mean. For an experimentalist it means that independent groups, with different samples and devices, find the same effect. By that standard the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes are mature: they have been reproduced repeatedly and extended to other platforms. What is still open is the mechanism and the role of disorder, which bear on the explanation and not on whether the phases exist. I would be more persuaded by your concern if the experimental record were contested. I also note, as you do, that either choice of third name leaves out someone with a documented claim, so this argument does not favour clocks over graphene; it only raises the cost of getting the citation wording right.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B013 first, argues that its main weakness is attribution and not stability of interpretation, and asks whether eight years is enough to separate the original discovery from a rapidly evolving family of moire effects. She also judges the overlap with the 2016 prize limited.
responses.response: Your question about separating the discovery from the moire family is the right test, and I think it is answered by scoping the citation to flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the first correlated and superconducting states there. Later fractional Chern insulators and other platforms are then neither claimed nor excluded. I agree with you that B013 does not depend on an open interpretive question, and that your argument that the 2016 overlap is limited is persuasive; I do not regard topology as ruled out by that prize. We differ on how the compound credit should weigh. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are a good trio, but you yourself list Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang as unresolved, and the three-name cap cannot honour both the two-dimensional and three-dimensional discoveries. In B025 one prediction and one experiment map onto three names, with Andrei the single contested seat. That is why I rank B025 ahead, and it is why B013 remains my first alternative, not a position I would resist.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B006 first, resists adding names, says the magic-wavelength idea and many-atom lattice regime are not contained in the comb or ion-clock prizes, and says attribution cleanliness should count above the number of members who ranked a candidate.
responses.response: I agree that attribution cleanliness is a legitimate criterion and that raw support counts are not a substitute for judgement; I tried to say the same in round 1. Your answer on novelty also moves me somewhat: the magic-wavelength concept and the many-atom regime are a distinct idea from the comb and the quantum-logic ion clock, and I would not oppose B006 strongly, which is why I now list it as an alternative. Two things still keep it behind B025 for me. First, the discovery content is a gain in precision of a quantity we already knew how to measure, whereas B025 opened a previously unexplored regime of correlated matter, and the committee should decide deliberately between those two kinds of prize. Second, the redefinition of the second remains undecided, and Lindroth is right that the prize should not hinge on it. On attribution I would say that B006 is cleaner on names, but B025 is not far behind once Bistritzer is kept, and the Andrei seat is a single, acknowledged compromise.

responses.point: Johansson moved toward the Bistritzer trio but wants the credit to Andrei kept open and the citation worded so that it does not imply nobody had seen flat-band signatures before 2018.
responses.response: I agree with the wording concern and have tried to reflect it. My citation names the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which are the two things the trio did, and it does not say that flat-band signatures were first seen in 2018. On the third seat, I keep Bistritzer because the continuum model is a joint result and the 2018 experiments were targeted at its magic angle, but I accept your point that Andrei's early scanning-probe work was real experimental evidence that the physics was there. I would not move to Andrei without revisiting the whole allocation, as I said in round 1. If the committee concluded the credit is experiment-led, I would want the argument stated openly rather than let the three-name cap decide by default, and I could accept it in that case.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, keeps B025 as the first alternative, and thinks the maturity gap, Andrei's claim and the unsettled mechanism mean the two cases are not equal.
responses.response: I agree that the two cases are not equal in maturity: B013 has almost twice the confirmation time, and I say so as the main reason I do not hold B025 with full confidence. I also agree with you and Olsson that the citation for B013 should be confined to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and that Mele should be kept. Where I part from you is on whether the open mechanism should count against the credited discovery, as against being a reason for careful wording. The Nobel record includes prizes for established effects whose microscopic explanation was still debated. I would count the mechanism against B025 only if there were contradictory experimental findings on the phases themselves, and I do not see any. Your first-alternative ranking for B025 and mine for B013 show that the two of us are weighing the same trade-off differently, not disagreeing about the science.

uncertainties: Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder make B025 premature relative to B013, a judgement about timing that I make as an experimentalist and cannot settle from the supplied evidence.

Whether Andrei should displace Bistritzer in the third seat; I rely on the supplied ballots and general recollection, not a verified historical record, and I would not support the swap without a fuller reconsideration of the allocation.

Whether the committee can apply a field-neutral rule on recent prizes in nearby areas (2016 topology, 2025 superconducting circuits, 2005 and 2012 metrology) consistently across B025, B013, B006 and B009.
Whether B013 should be preferred if the committee judges the Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit problem to be manageable through a tightly worded two-dimensional citation.
statement.conflict_note: As Chair I disclose documented connections to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur and a research field in gamma-ray and hard-X-ray instrumentation. B040 (gamma-ray burst afterglows) and B008 (IceCube) lie close to this field; I have moved neither into my final configuration and have dropped B040 from my alternatives, so I would not be arguing for either. No specific personal or institutional tie to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, or to the alternatives B013 and B006, is apparent from my profile. Subject-area distance from condensed matter is a limitation on my own judgement of B025, not a conflict, and I note it for colleagues to weigh.
